13.1.b:
A dislocation is the head leaving its cup; decades of progress have still not solved it, so first, how often and when.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how common is THA dislocation?"
- "About **1–3%** of primary hips dislocate, and **5–7%** of revisions."
- "Most dislocate in the **first 3 months**, while the soft tissues heal."
- "Late dislocations recur, so most of them end in revision."

### Incidence
Every hip surgeon will meet it.
- Primary THA (total hip arthroplasty) dislocates in ≈**1–3%** (Miller)
- The course quotes a round **3%**
- Revision hips dislocate more, at **5–7%**
- A meta-analysis of 4656 revisions found **9.04%** (Campbell)

### Timing of Dislocation
Timing matters, because it points to the cause.

#### Early Dislocation
- **75%** of dislocations happen in the first year (Prof Azzam)
- About **70%** of these come in the first **3 months**
- The capsule and muscles are still healing, and control is not back yet

#### Late Dislocation
- The risk then stays at ≈**1% per year** for 2–3 years
- After that it falls to ≈1% every **5 years**

| | Early dislocation | Late dislocation (>5 years) |
|---|---|---|
| Usual cause | position, healing soft tissue | wear, laxity |
| Recurrence | low if the parts are well placed | over half recur |
| Usual answer | **closed reduction** | most need **revision** |

MEMORY HOOK — the new tenant
- A new hip is like a new tenant: most trouble comes in the first **3 months** (≈70% of the first year's dislocations).

### Total Hip Arthroplasty versus Hemiarthroplasty after Femoral Neck Fracture
Here the implant you choose changes the risk.
- After a neck fracture, THA dislocates more than **hemiarthroplasty**
- So choose hemiarthroplasty when precautions will fail: **dementia**, Parkinson disease
- Choose THA for the **active** elderly, through an **anterior or anterolateral** approach
- In fracture patients over 75, the **direct lateral** approach dislocates least
- The posterior approach brings more re-operations for dislocation

13.2.b:
Now the why: four determinants explain almost every case.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "why did this hip dislocate?"
- "Four determinants: **design**, **position**, **soft-tissue tension**, **soft-tissue condition**."
- "The surgeon owns the first three; the patient owns the fourth."
- "The commonest surgical cause is **component malposition**."

### Determinants of Stability
Each one is a question to ask of a dislocated hip.

| Determinant | What it includes |
|---|---|
| **Design** (13.4) | head size, head–neck ratio, liner, constraint |
| **Position** (13.3) | stem, cup inclination, version |
| **Tension** (13.4) | femoral offset, trochanter, acetabular offset |
| **Condition** (below) | central, peripheral or myogenic deficits |

- It is usually **multifactorial**; patient factors can only be optimised
- **Malposition** is the commonest cause (Prof Azzam)
- Low annual volume means ≈**50%** more dislocations, so the learning curve matters

| Risk factors | Modifiable? | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Patient-related** | no, but can be optimised | spine, dysplasia, abductors, trochanter, high ROM |
| **Surgical** | yes, avoidable | malposition, fixation, approach, tension, capsular repair, head size, expertise |

MEMORY HOOK — DPTC
- **D**islocations **P**refer **T**ired **C**apsules: **D**esign, **P**osition, **T**ension, **C**ondition.

### Soft-Tissue Condition
No cup position can rescue muscles that cannot guard the hip.

#### Neuromuscular Deficits
- Here it means a disease of the nerves or muscles that control the abductors
- Those abductors are the main guards of the hip

| Type | Causes |
|---|---|
| **Central** | stroke, cerebellar dysfunction, L5 root compression or stenosis |
| **Peripheral** | **superior gluteal nerve** injury |
| **Myogenic / local** | myopathy, fatty atrophy (elderly), tumour, abscess, radiation, trauma |

#### Abductor Mechanism
- **Abductor insufficiency** leads to instability, so protect nerve and muscle
- The superior gluteal nerve runs between medius and minimus: split ≤**5 cm** above the trochanter (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 13.1 · 13.2
- It enters the posterior part of medius, so the safe split is the lower third above the trochanter (Prof Hazem)
- A lateral approach in inexperienced hands destroys the abductors → **Trendelenburg gait**
- Arthroplasty does not cure weakness, so record **abductor power and gait** first
- A neuromuscular hip gets **dual mobility** from the start; constraint is salvage (figure → 04)

#### Greater Trochanter
- **GT** (greater trochanter) non-union with proximal escape slackens the abductors → recurrent instability
- A fibrous non-union that stays in place is more stable
[[FIG: Fig 13.2 · 13.2

#### Developmental Dysplasia
- **DDH** (developmental dysplasia of the hip) dislocates more; soft tissue is the main issue
- The abductors are weak and contracted; rectus, **iliopsoas** and hamstrings are short
- The **capsule** is long and thick, partly lying where the head should sit
[[FIG: Fig 13.3 · 13.2

#### Range of Motion and External Forces
- A high **pre-operative ROM** (range of motion) means more instability
- **Trauma** is an outside force; **improper use** means extreme or forbidden positions
- The commonest culprits: **crossing the legs** and lying in **external rotation (ER)**
[[FIG: Fig 13.4 · 13.2

13.3.b:
Malposition is the commonest cause, so position gets its own part.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "where do you put the cup?"
- "Aim near **40°** of inclination; flat dislocates **posteriorly** in flexion, steep **superiorly**."
- "Anteverted escapes to the front; retroverted escapes to the back."
- "A stiff spine defeats a well-placed cup, so plan the spine before the hip."

### Acetabular Inclination
Inclination is how steeply the cup opens; both extremes fail.

#### Inclination and Direction of Dislocation
| Inclination | What happens |
|---|---|
| **<30°** (flat) | impingement early in **flexion** → **posterior** dislocation, worse with low anteversion |
| **30–50°** | balanced coverage and range: a compromise |
| **>50°** (steep) | easy **superior** dislocation, and a shorter jump distance |

- Older notes send the flat cup out **inferiorly**; Campbell says posteriorly, in flexion

MEMORY HOOK — the low ceiling
- A flat cup is a low ceiling: bend forward, the neck bangs into it, and the head levers out the back.

#### Lewinnek Safe Zone
- **Lewinnek** safe zone: inclination **40 ± 10°**, anteversion **15 ± 10°**
- Prof Sherif Khaled sets most of his own cups at **40°**; the Handbook templates at 45°
[[FIG: Fig 13.5 · 13.3
- But most early dislocations happen inside the zone (Campbell)
- Later work redefined it: inclination **27–47°**, anteversion **18–38°**
- Measuring inclination and version → 06 Post-op radiograph

#### Causes of Cup Malposition
- The zone is narrow, so errors come with **obesity**, a female pelvis, **lateral decubitus**
- Measured inclination changes with **pelvic tilt**, so standing differs from supine
- In theatre, the **transverse acetabular ligament** shows native cup orientation

### Stem Alignment
The stem tip matters too, because a tilted stem fails in more than one way.
- A **central** tip is ideal, valgus is acceptable, and varus is never accepted
- Varus raises bending on the cortex: fracture, dislocation and loosening follow
- A **lateralised** tip is itself a cause of instability

### Component Version
Version decides the direction of escape.

#### Version and Direction of Dislocation
- **Excess anteversion** lets the head escape **anteriorly**
- **Retroversion** makes the neck hit the rim in flexion and IR (internal rotation)
[[FIG: Fig 13.6 · 13.3
- So the head is levered out **posteriorly**

#### Combined Anteversion
- Stem anteversion adds to cup anteversion: together, **combined anteversion**
- One compensates the other, so judge them together

PITFALL — combined anteversion: which range?
- Course **30–50°**; Campbell **25–40°** (25–45° normal spine; Dorr goal 35°, range 25–50°); Miller 35–40°
- Say → "**combined anteversion ≈25–40°**, higher for a stiff spine (Campbell)"

#### Intraoperative Version
- A **lateral approach** sets the stem more retroverted; a **posterior** one, more anteverted (Prof Gobba)
[[FIG: Fig 13.7 · 13.3
- In the anterior approach, a cup **parallel to the neck cut** gives ideal combined anteversion
- Too much stem anteversion leaves the leg **internally rotated**
- In-toeing beyond **2 months** points to it

#### Distorted Native Version
| Native version | Seen in |
|---|---|
| More anteversion | **DDH**, juvenile RA (rheumatoid arthritis) |
| Less, or retroverted | old trauma, **Legg–Calvé–Perthes** (a low neck cut gives a neutral neck) |

- Anterior-wall **osteophytes** left behind make you misjudge cup version
- A shallow DDH socket gets a medialised cup; deficient walls tempt over-anteversion
[[FIG: Fig 13.8 · 13.3
- Fear of dislocation over-anteverts the cup, and the **broach** makes it worse
- The goal is native anatomy: excess either way brings impingement and a shorter life

### Spinopelvic Relationship
The pelvis moves when we sit, so a cup right standing may be wrong sitting.

#### Normal Spinopelvic Mobility
- From standing to sitting, the pelvis tilts back ≈**20–35°** (Prof Azzam)
[[FIG: Fig 13.9 · 13.3
- Its parameters: **pelvic incidence**, **sacral slope**, **pelvic tilt**
[[FIG: Fig 13.10 · 13.3
- Sitting tilt raises cup anteversion, so the anterior rim clears the neck

#### Stiff Spine and Flat Back
- **Fusion** or a stiff spine gives no tilt → unstable **sitting** (dynamic)
[[FIG: Fig 13.11 · 13.3
- Then the neck hits the anterior rim, and the head escapes **posteriorly**
- A **flat back** gives fixed posterior tilt → unstable **standing** (static)
- Then the front of the head is uncovered, and it escapes **anteriorly**
- After spinal fusion ≈**8%** are unstable despite good position, so plan the spine first
- Plan the deformity, spinal mobility and implant; **dual mobility** buys the extra stability

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Ante → anterior, retro → posterior · stiff spine sits out, flat back stands out**

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how does design keep a hip in?"
- "**Primary arc** is the range before impingement; **jump distance**, the travel to escape after it."
- "A **larger head** improves both; every rim or lip buys stability with range."
- "Restore **offset**; never buy stability by lengthening the leg."

### Primary Arc and Jump Distance
Every hip has two safety margins: before impingement and after it.
- **Primary arc** is the motion between opposite impingement points; it grows with **head–neck ratio**
[[FIG: Fig 13.12 · 13.4
- **Jump distance** ≈ **half the head diameter** (Campbell); 3–4 mm already matters
[[FIG: Fig 13.13 · 13.4
- After impingement, the head levers out safely, up to its radius
- The extra arc gained while it levers is the **lever range**
- So a bigger head jumps further and gains a wider lever range
- Years of **PE** (polyethylene) **wear** lower the rim, so a long-stable hip dislocates late

MEMORY HOOK — the fence
- The neck touching the rim is leaning on the fence; jump distance is the fence's height, about half the head's diameter.

### Femoral Head and Neck
A bigger head raises both margins; the neck decides when impingement starts.

#### Head Size and Head–Neck Ratio
- Larger heads are among the best measures against instability
[[FIG: Fig 13.14 · 13.4
- Heads of **36 mm** or more give more ROM and stability (Miller)
[[FIG: Fig 13.15 · 13.4
- Highly cross-linked PE made them practical, but metal heads raise **trunnion** concerns
- A thin neck raises the **head–neck ratio** and the ROM
[[FIG: Fig 13.16 · 13.4

#### Neck Design
- But thin necks have **fractured** after a year
- A **trapezoidal neck** is flattened in one plane, removing the impingement area
[[FIG: Fig 13.17 · 13.4
- Range serves **implant survival**, not sport; extremes bring wear and failure
[[FIG: Fig 13.18 · 13.4

### Skirts, Hoods and Liners
Each add-on raises one wall and costs range somewhere.

#### Skirted Heads and Acetabular Hoods
- A skirt lengthens the neck for offset, when the trial calls for a long head
- But a **skirted head** has a thicker neck, so it impinges early
- A **20° hood** cuts the primary arc from **100° to 80°** (Prof Gobba)
[[FIG: Fig 13.19 · 13.4
- The Handbook quotes a hood's loss as about **10°**
- A hood in the wrong place impinges early and dislocates the other way

#### Liner Options
- **Liner offset** pushes the head centre out, so head travel is longer
- An **elevated rim** goes where it dislocates: posterosuperior after a posterior approach
[[FIG: Fig 13.20 · 13.4
- But the high rim becomes a fulcrum in the opposite direction

#### Constrained Liners
- A **captive cup** has augments above and below the liner
[[FIG: Fig 13.21 · 13.4
- It allows only ≈**60°** of ROM; most stable, but loosens early in the young
- A constrained liner passes the **head's equator** and locks it in
[[FIG: Fig 13.22 · 13.4
- It cuts the primary arc, but it holds the head
- Avoid a **skirted head** with a constrained insert: it impinges early (Campbell)
- So neck–rim force goes into the **cup–bone interface** and ring → loosening, ring failure
[[FIG: Fig 13.23 · 13.4
- Case: well for a year, then the hardware broke and the cup moved

### Soft-Tissue Tension
A slack abductor is a weak abductor, so tension is the last surgical determinant.

#### Sources of Tension
- Tension keeps the femur and acetabulum together, so restore offset and leg length
- Tension comes from **femoral offset**, a lateralised cup, or **trochanteric advancement**
- How each lever works → 03 Hip biomechanics
- **Offset** is head centre to femoral axis; modular stems adjust it, rarely used
[[FIG: Fig 13.24 · 13.4
- Plain "offset" means medial offset; vertical offset matters too
- Tension is not one surgical step: it comes from planning size, position, offset and length

#### Consequences of Incorrect Offset
- Too little offset: the trochanter strikes → **bony impingement**, instability
- Too much: the iliotibial band rubs → **trochanteric bursitis**
[[FIG: Fig 13.25 · 13.4
- **Shortening** may cause dislocation, through lax soft tissue
- Its key cause is failing to restore horizontal and vertical offset
- A short head, a high cup or a deep stem also shorten the leg
- A malpositioned, unstable hip may be given a long neck on purpose
- Lengthening for stability trades dislocation for **leg-length inequality**
- Lengthening beyond **2.5 cm** risks nerve palsy, sciatic commonest

#### Intraoperative Assessment
- The **shuck test**: pull the reduced hip distally and watch the head piston
- Then test the extremes: ER with adduction, ER with abduction and extension
- Then flexion with adduction and IR: the posterior dislocating position
- Neck cut, leg length and templating → 05 Planning

- **Shortening** may cause dislocation, through lax soft tissue

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you work up a dislocated THA?"
- "Ask mechanism and timing, and **exclude infection** first."

- "AP and lateral films; **CT** for version; MARS MRI when films look normal."

### History
The story separates a trauma from a hip that fails on its own.
- **Mechanism**: trauma, or a bad position such as squatting or a low toilet
- Out during allowed activity, despite compliance? Then suspect the implant
- Then: recent or neglected, first or recurrent, time since surgery, approach
- Ask the position it came out in, and about recent **spine surgery**
- **Septic loosening** can present as recurrent dislocation → markers, then **aspirate**
- Aspirate when markers are positive, or on clinical judgement

### Clinical Examination
The limb shows the direction before any film.
- The signs are those of a native dislocation: sudden pain, lost function
- Confirm with **severe pain**, a rotated limb and LLD (limb-length discrepancy)

| Dislocation | Limb lies (Miller) |
|---|---|
| **Posterior** | short · flexed · adducted · internally rotated |
| **Anterior** | short · extended · externally rotated |

MEMORY HOOK — the shy one and the show-off
- Posterior is the shy hip: short, flexed, adducted, turned in. Anterior is the show-off: short, extended, turned out.

- Test the **sciatic** nerve (peroneal division): dorsiflexion before and after reduction
- Check pulses as well: the whole neurovascular status
- Check **cognition**: a brace cannot protect a non-compliant patient
- So that hip must be stable by design

### Imaging
Films answer the position questions of 13.3 and 13.4.

#### Plain Radiographs
- **AP pelvis** (both hips, proximal ⅓ femur) plus a **lateral**: AP alone cannot tell direction
[[FIG: Fig 13.26 · 13.6
- Add a **cross-table lateral**, and **standing and sitting** films for the spine

| Part | Look for |
|---|---|
| Head and neck | small head–neck ratio |
| Cup | steep, retroverted, position, head eccentric in the cup |
| Stem | medial and vertical offset vs the other side |
| Trochanter and bone | **GT** union, fractures |

- Films also hint at tension: a lateralised or medialised cup
- Soft-tissue diseases do not show on films, so they need their own tests

#### Offset and Version Assessment
- Compare offset only on **rotationally identical** views: match the obturator foramen
[[FIG: Fig 13.27 · 13.6
- On serial films, also look for cement–bone lucency and changed screws

#### Cross-Sectional Imaging
- **CT** finds malposition missed on films; it is most reliable for version
[[FIG: Fig 13.28 · 13.6
- Case: **55** years, AVN, THA; posterior dislocation on day 2, three times
[[FIG: Fig 13.29 · 13.6
- Her films looked acceptable, but CT showed malposition **>10°** → revise that component
- Recurrent dislocation with normal films points to the soft tissue
- Order **MRI with MARS** (metal artefact reduction sequence): abductors, osteolysis, wear

13.7.b:
Treatment follows the cause, from a gentle reduction to a salvage resection.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you treat a dislocated THA?"
- "**Reduce within 24 h**, closed under sedation; open only if closed fails."
- "Malposition or loosening → **revision**; otherwise liner, head or dual mobility."
- "A constrained liner and Girdlestone are the last steps."

### Treatment Timeline
Reduce first, fix what broke, then decide calmly.

| When | What (Handbook) |
|---|---|
| **<24 h** | reduction |
| **Days** | fix fractures |
| **Delayed** | conservative care or revision, with **infection out first** |

- Delay brings sciatic stretch, rim damage and contracture
- So a hip neglected beyond a few days is often irreducible closed

### Reduction
Most early hips go back closed, if handled gently.

#### Closed Reduction
- **Closed** reduction is best for early, first-time dislocations
- Force risks **periprosthetic fracture** and component dissociation, so use sedation
- GA (general anaesthesia) with relaxation is rarely needed
- But a dual mobility hip often fails under sedation: reduce it in theatre under GA (Campbell)

#### Reduction Technique
- Longitudinal traction under the **image intensifier**, then abduction
[[FIG: Fig 13.30 · 13.7
- **Allis**: supine, hip and knee flexed, in-line traction, assistant fixing the pelvis
- **Stimson**: prone, hip and knee flexed over the table edge, downward pressure
- Then check stability and nerves, take an X-ray, and brace

#### Open Reduction
- Open reduction, only then
- A PE liner may **dissociate**, even before arrival: the head sits eccentric in the shell
[[FIG: Fig 13.31 · 13.7
- Once a hard-on-soft joint is opened, **change the liner**: a notched rim wears fast
- The change is cheap and is not a full revision

### Bracing
A brace is offered after recurrence, but its value is doubtful.
- **Abduction brace**: 20° abduction, flexion ≤60°, for 6 weeks–3 months (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 13.32 · 13.7
- No proven benefit and poor compliance, so a **pillow** suffices (Prof Molham Mahmoud)
[[FIG: Fig 13.33 · 13.7
- Teach no squatting and no flexion beyond **90°**

PITFALL — brace in 20° of what?
- The Handbook says "≈20° flexion"; the course and Campbell say 20° abduction
- Say → "**abduction brace, 20° abduction, flexion limited to 60°, 6 weeks to 3 months**"

### Indications for Revision
Revise a hip that keeps coming out, or one with a defect you can see.

#### Indications
- **Recurrent instability**: more than 2 dislocations (Handbook)
- A **correctable defect** on films → revise after the 1st or 2nd
- Such defects: design, offset, a medialised or lateralised cup, retroversion
- No cause found → wait, because blind revision re-dislocates

#### Defining the Defect
- Position, offset, abductors and **impingement** (osteophyte, cement, heterotopic bone)
- **Malposition >10°** → revise that component; a constrained liner will not rescue it
- Case: recurrent at **3 years**, loose stem, aspiration negative → **long stem**
[[FIG: Fig 13.34 · 13.7

### Treatment by Cause
Exclude malposition and loosening first, because both need revision; then match the adjunct to the problem.

#### Cause-Specific Options
| Cause | Fix (Prof Azzam, Handbook) |
|---|---|
| Positional / soft-tissue imbalance (Dorr 1–2) | keep the components: liner exchange, elevated rim, larger head, dual mobility |
| Small head | larger head, tripolar or **dual mobility** liner |
| Lateralised stem | centralise the tip |
| Wrong inclination | revise to **30–50°** |
| Wrong version | **10–15°** anteversion (within Lewinnek) |
| Weak abductors | advance the GT inferolaterally; ↑ offset; soft-tissue reconstruction |
| Neuromuscular, multifactorial, idiopathic | **dual mobility** first; constrained cup as salvage |
| Malposition / loosening | **revision** |

- A larger head suits well-placed parts only; ceramic or metal on cross-linked PE, not metal-on-metal (Miller)
[[FIG: Fig 13.35 · 13.7
- Case: **65** years, neck fracture, dislocated at **3 months**: a clear mechanical cause
- So it got an extensive revision, with an excellent result
- A short leg that dislocates is revised to a **longer head**
- But shortening a long leg can destabilise the hip

#### Dual Mobility and Constrained Liners
- **Dual mobility** is often preferred: stable without locking the head (implant, intraprosthetic dislocation → 04)
- Keep it for patients whose problem needs it, not for a routine primary (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- **Tripolar** means dual mobility, not bipolar: a large PE head moves in a metal cup
- Inside that PE head sits a small metal head
- It suits the cognitively impaired patient, whose behaviour is unpredictable
- **Constrained** treats the symptom, costs motion and stresses fixation
[[FIG: Fig 13.36 · 13.7
- Use it only for a multifactorial or unclear cause, never over **10°** of malposition
- Case: fixed acetabular fracture, then THA; cup ≈**60°**, high centre
[[FIG: Fig 13.37 · 13.7
- Anteversion **15–20°** was acceptable; a long, high-offset neck levered on impingement
- It was revised with a constrained liner, which failed at a year
- A failed constrained liner → convert to **dual mobility**, and revise any malpositioned part
[[FIG: Fig 13.38 · 13.7
- In that case all parts came out, for a new acetabular reconstruction

#### Abductor Reconstruction
- A limp or a cane in the history points to weak abductors
- **Trochanteric advancement**: GT cut, fixed distally and laterally, abductors re-tensioned
[[FIG: Fig 13.39 · 13.7
- It needs no revision; if it fails, add offset with a longer neck or smaller neck–shaft angle
- A skirted head is then acceptable, though it costs some primary arc
- Proven **abductor deficiency** → **Achilles allograft** or a synthetic graft

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Reduce <24 h · >10° = revise · big head, dual mobility, advance · constrained last · Girdlestone**

### Girdlestone Resection Arthroplasty
When reconstruction keeps failing in a debilitated patient, the last answer removes the joint.
- For poor cognition, non-walkers, active infection, failed revisions (Handbook)
- The whole prosthesis comes out, leaving an empty head–neck space
[[FIG: Fig 13.40 · 13.7
- Girdlestone, an English surgeon, resected head and neck for septic arthritis in **1928**
- The leg ends **several cm short**; reimplantation later is worse than planned staging

MEMORY HOOK — nothing left to dislocate
- Girdlestone is the one hip that never dislocates again: there is nothing left to dislocate.

13.8.b:
Prevention is far cheaper than treatment, and it starts at the primary THA.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you prevent THA dislocation?"
- "Right patient and implant, restored anatomy, tensioned soft tissues."
- "Repair the posterior capsule and short external rotators."
- "Teach the precautions, and make the patient repeat them."

### Intraoperative Measures
Most dislocations are prevented before the wound is closed.

#### Surgical Approach
- The **posterior approach** dislocates most; the anterior less
[[FIG: Fig 13.41 · 13.8
- When risk factors pile up, choose the lower-risk approach

| Evidence (Prof Abo Elsoud) | Dislocation finding |
|---|---|
| Hip fracture, >75 years | posterior → more re-operation for dislocation |
| Augmented posterior repair | lower, but still above lateral |
| Swedish register, 156,000 hips | 1999–2006 posterior higher · 2007–2014 lateral = posterior |
| Posterior vs anterior (2016) | probably no difference |
| 16,000 patients | posterior **10×** lateral, **2×** anterior |

- The anterior approach opens only the anterior capsule
- Posterior capsule, rotators and glutei stay intact, so it almost never dislocates
- So it needs no restrictions; releasing the posterior capsule loses that benefit
- Obese or revision patients still suit the posterior approach
- The best approach is the one the surgeon does well

#### Capsular Repair
- Capsulectomy without repair is a major cause of early dislocation
- Repair capsule and short external rotators: **4.46% → 0.4%** (Campbell)
- Repair piriformis, rotators and capsule through the **gluteus medius tendon**
[[FIG: Fig 13.42 · 13.8
- The tendon holds better than drill holes; use non-absorbable sutures
- Add primary stability, a larger head and expertise

MEMORY HOOK — shut the back door
- After a posterior approach, sew the back door shut: repair takes dislocation from **4.46%** to **0.4%**.

### Postoperative Precautions
Each approach weakens one side, so the patient avoids the moves that open it.

#### Precautions by Approach
| Approach | Avoid | Leave the bed (Handbook) |
|---|---|---|
| **Posterior / posterolateral** | flexion >70–90° · IR · adduction · crossing legs | same side as surgery |
| **Anterior / anterolateral / lateral** | ER · hyperextension · adduction | opposite side |

- The forbidden move copies surgery: posterior hips are dislocated in IR, lateral ones in ER
- Leaving the bed on the operated side keeps that leg in ER, away from IR
- Posterior: flexion + adduction + IR together is the **dislocating position** (Prof Molham Mahmoud)
[[FIG: Fig 13.43 · 13.8
- So no low seats or bending: a **reacher**, a raised toilet seat, chairs with arms
[[FIG: Fig 13.44 · 13.8
- After **posterior capsular repair**, precautions can be relaxed safely

#### Patient Education
- The patient repeats the instructions at discharge and at follow-up
- Bed-transfer aids keep the patient independent without breaking the rules
- **Caregivers** are the safeguard in dementia, alcoholism or cognitive impairment
